newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists rap centre-right manifesto plans.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists rap centre-right manifesto plans.

text.p: French Socialists dismissed the ruling centre-right's new policy plans as more of the same failed medicine on Monday as a survey showed the coalition headed for a narrow majority in next month's election.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe on Sunday announced a 40-day flurry of legislation if his coalition wins re-election in the May 25-June 1 parliamentary election, promising spending caps to help qualify for a single European currency as well as tax cuts.

He also pledged to help cut record unemployment by cutting payroll charges on low wages, reduce the number of government ministries to 15, make working hours more flexible and pursue decentralisation.

"There is no change, this is the same policy. But as he is aware it is not very attractive. Juppe has stolen from the Socialist programme, especially on a cut in working hours," Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande said.

He said most of Juppe's policies had already been submitted to the National Assembly and accused the government of secretly planning a new round of cuts to qualify for the euro. "If the coalition wins, the austerity will be the 41st day," he said.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said earlier he would seek on Tuesday an election pact with the Communists, who oppose a planned single European currency favoured by the Socialists, and that the next government may include Communist ministers.
"It's an electoral accord, a text which if we succeed will express our way of tackling the election and the issues on which we agree, including criticism of the Right," he said.

Asked whether he planned to take Communists into government if the Socialists won, Jospin told Europe 1 radio: "The only problem is that of government cohesion. If there were to be a left-wing government, it could only be formed if there was only one clear political stance, including on Europe."
Hollande said the declaration would not seek to harmonise policies where the two parties were at odds, like over the euro currency.

The Socialists are in favour of the Euro although they have set conditions and refused further austerity steps if needed to reach the strict budget deficit criterion for European monetary union. The Communists oppose a single currency and want a referendum on the issue.

Jospin reiterated that he wanted a flexible view of the need to cut the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), preferring to look at the criterion as a "trend" instead of a fixed figure.
He also insisted that the southern European countries, notably Italy, should join the single currency from the start.
The newspaper Le Monde said Juppe's RPR party and its centrist allies in the UDF would unveil a manifesto on Tuesday fleshing out the policies outlined by Juppe.
It said the manifesto said aim is to "succeed in achieving the euro on January 1, 1999" and also to institute "a true social Europe which would avoid unfair competition among European countries."
The text notes the coalition's determination "to stabilise public spending so that it does not progress faster than inflation" but does not elaborate, the newspaper said.
The latest opinion poll showed the centre-right heading for a narrow majority but found more than one-third of voters could change their minds.

The BVA poll for France 2 television, Paris-Match magazine and Europe 1 radio said that if the election were held now, the ruling RPR-UDF coalition would win 296 of the 555 seats in metropolitan France, the Socialists 238, the Communists 18, the ecologists two and the extreme-right National Front one.
"The situation has never been so tight...There is a very great instability and uncertainty about voters' behaviour in the second round," said Pierre Giacometti of the IPSOS polling institute.
